title: Framing
hook: The same fact can push harder after someone changes its clothes.
counterintuition: Your reaction may be answering the wording, not the facts. A frame can make the same outcome feel like a gain, a loss, a rescue, or a threat.
tryThisNow: Before one decision today, rewrite the same fact as a gain and as a loss, then choose from the shared number underneath.
keyTakeaway: When wording changes your reaction, translate the choice into its opposite frame before deciding.

breakdown.fastRead:
The forecast grid glows on Joanne's wealth-adviser screen before a client call. One slide says the portfolio has a 90 percent chance of preserving capital. Another could say a 10 percent chance of loss. Joanne writes framing risk beside the grid.

Both statements can describe the same fact. The frame changes the emotional handle. Preserve feels calm. Loss feels sharp. If the decision changes when the wording changes, the wording is steering.

Same number, different pull.

The correction is to reverse the frame. Turn gains into losses, survival into mortality, discounts into costs, and ask whether the choice still holds.
breakdown.deepRead:
The forecast grid in Joanne's advisory dashboard shows the same retirement scenario in two ways. The first says the plan is likely to preserve capital. The second shows the chance that capital falls below the target. The client has not changed. The market has not changed. The sentence has changed.

Framing works because decisions arrive inside language. A plan can be worded by what it saves or what it risks, by what you gain or what you forgo, by how many succeed or how many fail. The facts may stay fixed while the emotional path shifts. The mind often reacts before it notices the translation.

The frame is part of the choice.

Albert sees the same issue in a lead-test average review. A donor pledge card sits beside a school water report. One draft says 95 percent of samples are below the threshold. Another says 5 percent exceed it. Albert marks wording risk on the card because the same average may produce either relief or alarm depending on which side of the threshold the sentence lights up.

The goal is not to become numb to wording. Wording matters because people need to understand risk. The discipline is to make the hidden twin visible. If the gain frame makes you say yes, check the loss frame. If the loss frame makes you panic, check the gain frame. Then decide from the underlying trade-off.

A fair frame lets the same fact survive translation.
breakdown.fullRead:
The shift roster on Justin's ferry maintenance table is smudged with engine grease. A repair option is described as keeping 80 percent of sailings on schedule during the next month. The operations lead likes it. Justin writes medicine frame risk on the roster and rewrites the line: one in five sailings will still be disrupted.

Nothing factual has changed. The first frame highlights success. The second highlights failure. In medicine, the same pattern is familiar: a treatment described by survival can feel different from one described by mortality. Tversky and Kahneman's work on the framing of decisions made that point hard to ignore. People can shift choices when the same outcome is cast as lives saved or lives lost.

Which version would you choose if the sentence were reversed?

Justin asks that before the ferry vote. The team keeps both frames on the table. Schedule preserved. Sailings disrupted. Cost avoided. Cost paid. Passenger complaints reduced. Passenger complaints remaining. The repair option may still be right, but it no longer wins by showing only the bright side of the same number.

You can feel this in an award-to-sales design review. You are holding a risk register while Mary compares two ways to describe a product badge. One says winners convert 18 percent better. The other says non-winners lose 15 percent of expected sales lift. Mary must decide whether choice frame risk is changing the design decision before the same evidence is examined both ways.

Framing also hides inside labels. A fee can be a service charge or a penalty. A discount can be savings or money left unclaimed. A policy can be described by households helped or households still waiting. A volcano tourism booking report can say 98 percent of trips run safely or 2 percent face cancellation and evacuation risk. The sentence does not merely report the fact. It points the reader toward a feeling.

The strongest frame is often the one that sounds like plain description. Safe, improved, protected, delayed, denied, and rescued all carry a tilt. None of those words is automatically dishonest. The issue is whether the matching frame is missing. A fair memo lets the reader see what is gained and what remains at risk.

Good decisions do not require sterile language. They require honest translation. Put the opposing frame beside the first one. Ask whether the action changes. If it does, slow down and find the common number beneath the two sentences.

When wording changes your reaction, translate the choice into its opposite frame before deciding.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Framing makes presentation feel like evidence. Readers need to reverse the wording so the same facts can be judged without the first label choosing for them.

reviewCards.front: A fact is framed as a gain. What should you do?
reviewCards.back: Rewrite it as the equivalent loss, then decide from the shared number.

reviewCards.front: Why can true wording still mislead?
reviewCards.back: A true frame can emphasize one emotional side of the same fact while hiding the equivalent opposite frame.
Translate survival into mortality, or mortality into survival, before choosing.

reviewCards.front: How do you know framing is steering?
reviewCards.back: If your decision changes when the same fact is worded the opposite way, the frame is influencing you.

reviewCards.front: What is the core correction for framing?
reviewCards.back: Put opposing frames beside each other and choose from the underlying fact.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to translate decisions out of their first wording. The habit is to write the opposite frame and make the shared number visible before choosing.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a result is described as preservation or gain, then I will also write the loss version.
If a risk is described by survival or success, then I will also write mortality, failure, or remaining harm.
If a report highlights people helped, then I will also show people still waiting or affected.
If wording changed the room's reaction, then I will identify the shared fact underneath both frames.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, take one number you plan to present and write its gain frame and loss frame before sharing it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review a decision memo and add the missing opposite frame beside every key percentage.
